claim: Hunger is a biological drive which can promote unhealthy dietary decisions.
source: Hunger is a biological drive which can promote unhealthy dietary decisions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: Participants' preference for tasty over healthy food items was amplified by hunger.
source: Confirming our preregistered hypotheses, participants' preference for tasty over healthy food items was amplified by hunger.
evidence: This is a preregistered hypothesis that was confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: Attention mediated the influence of hunger on dietary decisions.
source: Attention mediated this influence of hunger, as hungry participants focused more on tasty options, leading them to make less healthy decisions.
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis reported in the results section.

claim: Hungry participants focused more on tasty options.
source: Attention mediated this influence of hunger, as hungry participants focused more on tasty options, leading them to make less healthy decisions.
evidence: This is supported by eye-tracking data showing increased dwell time on tasty options under hunger.

claim: An extension of the multi-attribute attentional drift diffusion model best explained choice and response times.
source: Rigorous model comparisons revealed that an extension of the recently proposed multi-attribute attentional drift diffusion model best explained choice and response times.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison using DIC values reported in Table 1.

claim: Hunger increased the relative taste compared to health weight.
source: According to this model, hunger did not only increase the relative taste compared to health weight, but it also increased the fixation-related discounting of health but not taste information.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates from the maaDDM2φ model shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Hunger increased the fixation-related discounting of health but not taste information.
source: According to this model, hunger did not only increase the relative taste compared to health weight, but it also increased the fixation-related discounting of health but not taste information.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates from the maaDDM2φ model shown in Figure 5f and 5g.

claim: Health information such as nutritional scores on food options can increase the number of healthy choices.
source: For example, it has been shown that health information such as nutritional scores on food options (Rramani et al., 2020) or health primes (Hare et al., 2011; Sullivan and Huettel, 2021) can increase the number of healthy choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A hungry decision maker is more likely to make unhealthy decisions.
source: On the other hand, a hungry decision maker is more likely to make unhealthy decisions (Cheung et al., 2017; Hoefling and Strack, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A preference for energy dense foods was adaptive and ensured survival under conditions of scarcity.
source: Evolutionarily, a preference for energy dense foods was adaptive and ensured survival under conditions of scarcity (Hanßen et al., 2022; Mattson, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on evolutionary perspectives.

claim: The food environment in Western societies has become increasingly obesogenic.
source: While the food environment in Western societies has become increasingly obesogenic, with high caloric food options being affordable and easily available, the neurobiological mechanism continues to reward the consumption of energy dense foods contributing to a global surge in obesity rates (Mitchell et al., 2011; World Health Organization, 2021; Lobstein et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and WHO reports.

claim: Under hunger, high-caloric food options are viewed more rewarding.
source: Consistent with the evolutionary mechanism that reinforces high-energy dense food options, behavioral (Cameron et al., 2014; Cheung et al., 2017; Epstein et al., 2003), and neuroimaging studies (e.g. Banica et al., 2023; Dagher, 2012; Malik et al., 2008) indicate that under hunger (high-caloric) food options are viewed more rewarding, are more frequently chosen over healthy alternatives, and draw more attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral and neuroimaging studies.

claim: Under hunger, high-caloric food options are more frequently chosen over healthy alternatives.
source: Consistent with the evolutionary mechanism that reinforces high-energy dense food options, behavioral (Cameron et al., 2014; Cheung et al., 2017; Epstein et al., 2003), and neuroimaging studies (e.g. Banica et al., 2023; Dagher, 2012; Malik et al., 2008) indicate that under hunger (high-caloric) food options are viewed more rewarding, are more frequently chosen over healthy alternatives, and draw more attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral and neuroimaging studies.

claim: Under hunger, high-caloric food options draw more attention.
source: Consistent with the evolutionary mechanism that reinforces high-energy dense food options, behavioral (Cameron et al., 2014; Cheung et al., 2017; Epstein et al., 2003), and neuroimaging studies (e.g. Banica et al., 2023; Dagher, 2012; Malik et al., 2008) indicate that under hunger (high-caloric) food options are viewed more rewarding, are more frequently chosen over healthy alternatives, and draw more attention.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral and neuroimaging studies.

claim: Meta-analyses have revealed an attentional bias towards food versus neutral stimuli, which was further amplified by hunger state.
source: Meta-analyses have revealed an attentional bias towards food versus neutral stimuli, which was further amplified by hunger state (Hardman et al., 2021; Pool et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analyses.

claim: There is a strong positive association between the time people spend looking at a food option and the probability with which they choose it.
source: This work has provided evidence for a strong positive association between the time people spend looking at a (food) option and the probability with which they choose it (Krajbich, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is no study modeling attention and choice dynamics under different hunger states.
source: To the best of our knowledge, there is no study modeling attention and choice dynamics under different hunger states leaving the cognitive and attentional mechanisms underlying hunger-driven food choice unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: 70 participants completed a binary food choice task in hungry and sated states while their eye movements were being recorded.
source: To fill this gap, we conducted a within-subject experiment, in which 70 participants completed a binary food choice task in hungry and sated states while their eye movements were being recorded (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: The considered attributes of the binary options were taste and health as represented by food images and their nutritional scores, respectively.
source: The considered attributes of the binary options were taste and health as represented by food images and their nutritional scores, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants were more likely to choose tasty over healthy food items.
source: Confirming our preregistered hypotheses, participants were more likely to choose tasty over healthy food items, and this difference was amplified under hunger.
evidence: This is a preregistered hypothesis confirmed by the data.

claim: The difference in preference for tasty over healthy food items was amplified under hunger.
source: Confirming our preregistered hypotheses, participants were more likely to choose tasty over healthy food items, and this difference was amplified under hunger.
evidence: This is a preregistered hypothesis confirmed by the data.

claim: Participants focused more on taste information under hunger, leading them to make less healthy decisions.
source: Notably, attention mediated the influence of hunger on dietary decisions, as participants focused more on taste information under hunger, leading them to make less healthy decisions.
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis and eye-tracking data.

claim: The multi-attribute attentional DDM was extended to allow the discounting of unattended information to differ across different attributes.
source: Critically, we extended the recently proposed multi-attribute attentional DDM (Yang and Krajbich, 2023) to allow the discounting of unattended information to differ across different attributes (here: taste vs. health).
evidence: This describes the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The extended model provided the best account of the behavioral data.
source: This model not only provided the best account of our behavioral data, but also revealed a twofold mechanism, wherein hunger affects valuation of choice options by shifting the relative weighting of taste information and by exacerbating the attentional discounting of health (but not taste) information.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results in Table 1.

claim: Hunger affects valuation of choice options by shifting the relative weighting of taste information.
source: This model not only provided the best account of our behavioral data, but also revealed a twofold mechanism, wherein hunger affects valuation of choice options by shifting the relative weighting of taste information and by exacerbating the attentional discounting of health (but not taste) information.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates from the maaDDM2φ model.

claim: Hunger exacerbates the attentional discounting of health but not taste information.
source: This model not only provided the best account of our behavioral data, but also revealed a twofold mechanism, wherein hunger affects valuation of choice options by shifting the relative weighting of taste information and by exacerbating the attentional discounting of health (but not taste) information.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter estimates from the maaDDM2φ model.

claim: The change in hunger ratings between the last and first time point differed across conditions.
source: The RM-ANOVA indicated that the change in hunger ratings between the last and first time point differed across conditions (F(1)=26.31, p<.001, d=0.708).
evidence: This is supported by RM-ANOVA results.

claim: The hunger state manipulation had the desired effect on the subjective feeling of hunger.
source: Thus, our hunger state manipulation had the desired effect on the subjective feeling of hunger.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of hunger ratings.

claim: There were no effects of hunger state on positive and negative affect across timepoints.
source: Notably, there were no effects of hunger state on positive and negative affect across timepoints (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of PANAS data reported in the appendix.

claim: 81% of variance in food measures was explained by two components.
source: Results revealed that 81% of variance was explained by two components, the first loading positively on caloric information (subjective and objective) and negatively on health information (subjective health rating and Nutri-Score), while the second one loaded positively on taste and wanting (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by PCA results shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The first principal component loaded positively on caloric information and negatively on health information.
source: Results revealed that 81% of variance was explained by two components, the first loading positively on caloric information (subjective and objective) and negatively on health information (subjective health rating and Nutri-Score), while the second one loaded positively on taste and wanting (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by PCA results shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The second principal component loaded positively on taste and wanting.
source: Results revealed that 81% of variance was explained by two components, the first loading positively on caloric information (subjective and objective) and negatively on health information (subjective health rating and Nutri-Score), while the second one loaded positively on taste and wanting (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by PCA results shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Loadings of taste measures on the health component and loadings of health measures on the taste component were low suggesting independence of these factors.
source: Importantly, loadings of taste measures on the health component and loadings of health measures on the taste component were low suggesting independence of these factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA results.

claim: In both conditions, a larger value difference with respect to taste was predictive of tasty choice.
source: In both conditions, a larger value difference (VD) with respect to taste was predictive of tasty choice (Figure 2c), while a larger VD with respect to health was predictive of healthy choice, particularly in the sated condition (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the choice probability plots in Figure 2c.

claim: A larger value difference with respect to health was predictive of healthy choice, particularly in the sated condition.
source: In both conditions, a larger value difference (VD) with respect to taste was predictive of tasty choice (Figure 2c), while a larger VD with respect to health was predictive of healthy choice, particularly in the sated condition (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is supported by the choice probability plots in Figure 2d.

claim: RT was highest for choices in which taste ratings were similar for both options.
source: With respect to response time (RT), we found that RT was highest for choices in which taste ratings were similar for both options (Figure 2e), while health value did not affect RT (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by the RT plots in Figure 2e.

claim: Health value did not affect RT.
source: With respect to response time (RT), we found that RT was highest for choices in which taste ratings were similar for both options (Figure 2e), while health value did not affect RT (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by the RT plots in Figure 2f.

claim: The GLMM of RT indicated an average RT of 2.748 s.
source: The GLMM of RT indicated an average RT of 2.748 s (SE = 0.096).
evidence: This is supported by GLMM analysis of RT data.

claim: Tasty choices were associated with faster decisions, decreasing RT by 0.15 s.
source: Tasty choices were associated with faster decisions, decreasing RT by 0.15 s (SE = 0.018, p<0f.001).
evidence: This is supported by GLMM analysis of RT data.

claim: Participants preferred tasty over healthy options, and that this preference was amplified under hunger.
source: Altogether, we found that participants preferred tasty over healthy options, and that this preference was amplified under hunger.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the choice analysis.

claim: Tasty choices were faster in general.
source: While tasty choices were faster in general, we did not find an effect of hunger state on RT.
evidence: This is supported by the GLMM analysis of RT data.

claim: There was no effect of hunger state on RT.
source: While tasty choices were faster in general, we did not find an effect of hunger state on RT.
evidence: This is supported by the GLMM analysis of RT data.

claim: Dwell time is an important predictor of choice and RT.
source: Finally, our GLMMs indicate that dwell time is an important predictor of choice and RT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GLMM results.

claim: Looking longer at the tasty option predicted tasty choice.
source: In line with previous work (Gluth et al., 2018; Krajbich et al., 2010; Weilbächer et al., 2021; Yang and Krajbich, 2023), our choice GLMM indicated that looking longer at the tasty option predicted tasty choice.
evidence: This is supported by GLMM analysis and previous literature.

claim: The effect of dwell time on choice was observed in both conditions to a very similar degree.
source: This effect was observed in both conditions to a very similar degree (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3a showing similar slopes for both conditions.

claim: Participants were much more likely to look at food images than the Nutri-Scores in both conditions.
source: When analyzing dwell time on the attribute level, however, there was a significant condition difference: Although participants were much more likely to look at food images (taste attribute) than the Nutri-Scores (health attribute) in both conditions, this difference was even more pronounced in the hungry compared to the sated state (t(69)=2.595, P=.006, d=0.312; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3b.

claim: The difference in dwell time between food images and Nutri-Scores was even more pronounced in the hungry compared to the sated state.
source: When analyzing dwell time on the attribute level, however, there was a significant condition difference: Although participants were much more likely to look at food images (taste attribute) than the Nutri-Scores (health attribute) in both conditions, this difference was even more pronounced in the hungry compared to the sated state (t(69)=2.595, P=.006, d=0.312; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 3b.

claim: The effect of hunger on attribute-level dwell time remained significant after excluding outlier data.
source: This effect remained significant after excluding outlier data (t(68)=2.392, P=.01, d=0.29).
evidence: This is supported by robustness analysis.

claim: Attention was predictive of choice.
source: Altogether, the eye-tracking analyses demonstrated that attention was predictive of choice, and hungry participants' preference for tasty foods was reflected in their dwell time.
evidence: This is a summary of the eye-tracking findings.

claim: Hungry participants' preference for tasty foods was reflected in their dwell time.
source: Altogether, the eye-tracking analyses demonstrated that attention was predictive of choice, and hungry participants' preference for tasty foods was reflected in their dwell time.
evidence: This is a summary of the eye-tracking findings.

claim: Attention emerged as a pivotal mediator of the relationship between hunger state and food choice.
source: Finally, attention emerged as a pivotal mediator of the relationship between hunger state and food choice.
evidence: This is a summary of the mediation analysis findings.

claim: Models without starting point consistently outperformed models with starting point.
source: Initial model comparison revealed that there was no evidence for a starting point effect, as models without starting point consistently outperformed models with starting point.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results in Table 1.

claim: Hunger increased the weight of taste information relative to health information.
source: Further inspection of differences in the maaDDM's parameter estimates between the hungry and sated conditions suggested that hunger increased the weight of taste information relative to health information and exacerbated attribute-wise attentional discounting i.e., lower estimates of parameter ϕ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by parameter estimates shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hunger exacerbated attribute-wise attentional discounting.
source: Further inspection of differences in the maaDDM's parameter estimates between the hungry and sated conditions suggested that hunger increased the weight of taste information relative to health information and exacerbated attribute-wise attentional discounting i.e., lower estimates of parameter ϕ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by parameter estimates shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maaDDM2ϕ model provided a substantially improved model fit compared to the maaDDM and all other models.
source: Remarkably, this model provided a substantially improved model fit compared to the maaDDM and all other models (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by DIC values in Table 1.

claim: The maaDDM2ϕ model provides an exquisite account of the choice and RT data.
source: Moreover, the posterior predictive checks of this model indicated that it provides an exquisite account of the choice and RT data (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by posterior predictive checks shown in Figure 4.

claim: The taste preference was credibly higher under hunger.
source: Critically, this preference was credibly higher under hunger (HDI=[0.122, 0.642]; Figure 5a), as the HDI of the effect of hunger did not include 0.
evidence: This is supported by parameter estimates shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Individuals prefer tasty over healthy food options.
source: We found that individuals prefer tasty over healthy food options, and that this preference is amplified by hunger state.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The preference for tasty over healthy food options is amplified by hunger state.
source: We found that individuals prefer tasty over healthy food options, and that this preference is amplified by hunger state.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Taste was weighted more than health in both conditions, but especially in the hungry condition.
source: This pattern was also reflected in our modeling analyses, revealing that taste was weighted more than health in both, but especially in the hungry condition.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling findings.

claim: The cognitive mechanism underlying the influence of hunger state on food choice is driven by a shift in attention.
source: Our mediation analysis suggests that the cognitive mechanism underlying the influence of hunger state on food choice is driven by a shift in attention.
evidence: This is a summary of the mediation analysis findings.

claim: Hungry individuals pay more attention to tasty food options in general and the taste attribute in particular.
source: Specifically, hungry individuals pay more attention to tasty food options in general and the taste attribute in particular, which in turn increases the probability of tasty choices.
evidence: This is a summary of the eye-tracking findings.

claim: Paying more attention to tasty food options increases the probability of tasty choices.
source: Specifically, hungry individuals pay more attention to tasty food options in general and the taste attribute in particular, which in turn increases the probability of tasty choices.
evidence: This is a summary of the eye-tracking findings.

claim: The cognitive modeling analyses demonstrated increased attentional discounting of the health attribute under hunger.
source: Again, our cognitive modeling analyses integrated these findings, demonstrating increased attentional discounting of the health attribute under hunger.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling findings.

claim: Hunger affects dietary choice.
source: First, in line with previous research (Cheung et al., 2017; Otterbring, 2019; Read and Leeuwen, 1998) we demonstrate that hunger affects dietary choice.
evidence: This is supported by the current study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Participants were more likely to choose options that were rated more tasty than healthy.
source: Participants were more likely to choose options that were rated more tasty than healthy, for which reported higher wanting, and that contained higher caloric content.
evidence: This is supported by the choice analysis.

claim: Participants were more likely to choose options for which they reported higher wanting.
source: Participants were more likely to choose options that were rated more tasty than healthy, for which reported higher wanting, and that contained higher caloric content.
evidence: This is supported by the choice analysis.

claim: Participants were more likely to choose options that contained higher caloric content.
source: Participants were more likely to choose options that were rated more tasty than healthy, for which reported higher wanting, and that contained higher caloric content.
evidence: This is supported by the choice analysis.

claim: Higher taste ratings were strongly predictive of choice across conditions.
source: Moreover, our findings indicate that higher taste ratings were strongly predictive of choice across conditions, whereas higher health ratings only predicted choice in the sated condition, albeit less influential than taste ratings (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by the choice probability plots in Figure 2c and d.

claim: Higher health ratings only predicted choice in the sated condition.
source: Moreover, our findings indicate that higher taste ratings were strongly predictive of choice across conditions, whereas higher health ratings only predicted choice in the sated condition, albeit less influential than taste ratings (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by the choice probability plots in Figure 2c and d.

claim: Health ratings were less influential than taste ratings in predicting choice.
source: Moreover, our findings indicate that higher taste ratings were strongly predictive of choice across conditions, whereas higher health ratings only predicted choice in the sated condition, albeit less influential than taste ratings (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is supported by the choice probability plots in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The relative taste weight was larger in both conditions and particularly in the hungry condition.
source: Crucially, our modeling analyses endorsed this account: across models, we demonstrate that the relative taste weight was larger in both conditions and particularly in the hungry condition.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results.

claim: Hunger elevated the bids in a food bidding task.
source: This also aligns with results from a food bidding task (Fisher and Rangel, 2014), wherein the authors find that hunger elevated the bids and speculate that this effect was driven by an increased taste but not health valuation of food items.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The effect of hunger on bids in a food bidding task was driven by an increased taste but not health valuation of food items.
source: This also aligns with results from a food bidding task (Fisher and Rangel, 2014), wherein the authors find that hunger elevated the bids and speculate that this effect was driven by an increased taste but not health valuation of food items.
evidence: This is a speculation from a cited study.

claim: Valuation is influenced by the attributes underlying decision weights.
source: Second, we show that the valuation is not only influenced by the attributes underlying decision weights, but moreover by attention.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Valuation is influenced by attention.
source: Second, we show that the valuation is not only influenced by the attributes underlying decision weights, but moreover by attention.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Hunger state predicts overall less dwell time on the healthy option.
source: Behaviorally, we show that attention mediates the impact of hunger state on food choice, such that hunger state predicts overall less dwell time on the healthy option, thereby increasing the probability of tasty choice.
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis.

claim: Less dwell time on the healthy option increases the probability of tasty choice.
source: Behaviorally, we show that attention mediates the impact of hunger state on food choice, such that hunger state predicts overall less dwell time on the healthy option, thereby increasing the probability of tasty choice.
evidence: This is supported by the mediation analysis.

claim: Participants, especially when hungry, spent much more time on food images compared to Nutri-Scores.
source: Upon closer examination of attention allocation to the respective attributes, we show that participants, especially when hungry, spent much more time on food images compared to Nutri-Scores.
evidence: This is supported by the eye-tracking analysis.

claim: Food images were more important for deciding, as indicated by the relative weight parameter being larger than 0.5.
source: We see two explanations for the excessively high proportion of dwell time on food images compared to Nutri-Scores: First, food images were more important for deciding, as indicated by the relative weight parameter being larger than 0.5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: People pay more attention to more important attributes.
source: Consequently and in line with previous work (Orquin et al., 2021), people pay more attention to more important attributes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Food images contain more complex information than Nutri-Scores.
source: Second, food images contain more complex information.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the nature of the stimuli.

claim: Extracting taste information from a food image can be seen as a complex inference process.
source: Whereas extracting taste information from a food image can be seen as a complex inference process, a (color-coded) nutritional score provides salient and easily discernible evidence about a product's healthiness and consequently requires less dwell time.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cognitive processes involved.

claim: A color-coded nutritional score provides salient and easily discernible evidence about a product's healthiness.
source: Whereas extracting taste information from a food image can be seen as a complex inference process, a (color-coded) nutritional score provides salient and easily discernible evidence about a product's healthiness and consequently requires less dwell time.
evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of the Nutri-Score.

claim: Nutritional scores can promote healthy choice despite proportionally little dwell time.
source: This account is supported by studies showing that nutritional scores can promote healthy choice despite proportionally little dwell time (e.g. Bialkova et al., 2014; Gabor et al., 2020; Rramani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The attentional discounting of the health attribute but not the taste attribute was amplified under hunger.
source: Consistent with the above-mentioned attribute-specific effect of hunger on choices, we found that the attentional discounting of the health attribute but not the taste attribute was amplified under hunger, such that unattended nutritional information had a blunted influence on the evidence accumulation process.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results.

claim: Unattended nutritional information had a blunted influence on the evidence accumulation process under hunger.
source: Consistent with the above-mentioned attribute-specific effect of hunger on choices, we found that the attentional discounting of the health attribute but not the taste attribute was amplified under hunger, such that unattended nutritional information had a blunted influence on the evidence accumulation process.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results.

claim: Hunger could impede a person's ability or willingness to maintain health considerations in working memory when attention is currently drawn to the tasty food stimulus.
source: Given related work on the malleability of attentional discounting on mnemonic demands (Eum et al., 2023; Weilbächer et al., 2021), we speculate that hunger could impede a person's ability or willingness to maintain health considerations in working memory when attention is currently drawn to the tasty food stimulus.
evidence: This is a speculation based on related work.

claim: Hungry participants were more likely to choose items which they rated higher in terms of tastiness, wanting and caloric content.
source: In essence, and in line with a large body of literature (e.g. Garlasco et al., 2019; Otterbring, 2019; Read and Leeuwen, 1998), hungry participants were more likely to choose items which they rated higher in terms of tastiness, wanting and caloric content.
evidence: This is supported by supplementary analyses and previous literature.

claim: The pivotal role of attention was established in the exploratory wanting and calorie analyses.
source: Importantly, the pivotal role of attention was also established in the exploratory wanting and calorie analyses.
evidence: This is supported by supplementary analyses.

claim: Two factors representing tastiness and healthiness aspects explain 81% of the variance in the data.
source: Moreover, we performed a PCA to identify the major components that drive food choices, finding that two factors representing tastiness and healthiness aspects explain 81% of the variance in the data.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA results.

claim: The PCA justifies describing and studying dietary choices by means of taste and health attributes.
source: We see this as a justification to describe and study dietary choices by means of these two attributes, essentially following a series of previous studies in our field (e.g. Hutcherson and Tusche, 2022; Maier et al., 2020; Rramani et al., 2020; Sullivan and Huettel, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the PCA results and previous literature.

claim: The present results support the twofold effect of hunger state on the cognitive mechanisms underlying choice.
source: The present results and supplementary analyses clearly support the twofold effect of hunger state on the cognitive mechanisms underlying choice.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: There are potential demand effects arising from the within-subject Protein-shake manipulation.
source: However, we acknowledge potential demand effects arising from the within-subject Protein-shake manipulation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation.

claim: Labeling water to decrease or increase hunger affected participants subsequent hunger ratings and food valuations.
source: A recent study (Khalid et al., 2024) showed that labeling water to decrease or increase hunger affected participants subsequent hunger ratings and food valuations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The absence of a starting point effect speaks against any prior bias in participants due to any demand effects.
source: The absence of a starting point effect in our data speaks against any prior bias in participants due to any demand effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Both homeostatic and hedonic mechanisms drive eating behavior.
source: From a neurobiological perspective, both homeostatic and hedonic mechanisms drive eating behavior.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Homeostatic mechanisms regulate eating behavior based on energy needs.
source: While homeostatic mechanisms regulate eating behavior based on energy needs, hedonic mechanisms operate independent of caloric deficit (Alonso-Alonso et al., 2015; Lowe and Butryn, 2007; Saper et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hedonic mechanisms operate independent of caloric deficit.
source: While homeostatic mechanisms regulate eating behavior based on energy needs, hedonic mechanisms operate independent of caloric deficit (Alonso-Alonso et al., 2015; Lowe and Butryn, 2007; Saper et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Participants' preference for tasty high-caloric food options in the hungry condition aligns with a drive for energy restoration.
source: Participants' preference for tasty high-caloric food options in the hungry condition aligns with a drive for energy restoration and could thus be taken as an adaptive response to signals from the body.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Participants preferred less healthy options also in the sated condition.
source: On the other hand, our data shows that participants preferred less healthy options also in the sated condition.
evidence: This is supported by the choice data.

claim: Hedonic drivers could predominate in the sated condition indicating potentially maladaptive decision-making.
source: Here, hedonic drivers could predominate indicating potentially maladaptive decision-making that could lead to adverse health outcomes if sustained.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Participants in the sated condition showed reduced attentional discounting of health information.
source: Notably, our modeling analyses indicated that participants in the sated condition showed reduced attentional discounting of health information, which poses potential for attention-based intervention strategies to counter hedonic hunger.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results.

claim: Reduced attentional discounting of health information poses potential for attention-based intervention strategies to counter hedonic hunger.
source: Notably, our modeling analyses indicated that participants in the sated condition showed reduced attentional discounting of health information, which poses potential for attention-based intervention strategies to counter hedonic hunger.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Focusing attention on health aspects increased healthy choice.
source: This has been investigated, for example, in behavioral (Barakchian et al., 2021; Bucher et al., 2016; Cheung et al., 2017; Sullivan and Huettel, 2021), eye-tracking (Schomaker et al., 2022; Vriens et al., 2020) and neuroimaging studies (Hare et al., 2011; Hutcherson and Tusche, 2022) showing that focusing attention on health aspects increased healthy choice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mechanism through which health cues enhance healthy choice is shaped by increased value computations in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex when cue and choice are conflicting.
source: For example, Hutcherson and Tusche, 2022 compellingly demonstrated that the mechanism through which health cues enhance healthy choice is shaped by increased value computations in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) when cue and choice are conflicting (i.e. health cue, tasty choice).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Drawing people's attention towards health information will promote healthy choice by mitigating the increased attentional discounting of such information in the presence of tempting food stimuli.
source: In the context of hunger, these findings together with our analyses suggest that drawing people's attention towards health information will promote healthy choice by mitigating the increased attentional discounting of such information in the presence of tempting food stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and previous research.

claim: The valuation of food options under hunger is compromised by a relatively lower weighting and a stronger attentional discounting of health information.
source: Our extension of the multi-attribute attentional DDM revealed that the valuation of food options under hunger is compromised by a relatively lower weighting and a stronger attentional discounting of health information.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The modeling extension represents a general contribution to advance research on multi-attribute decision-making.
source: This modeling extension represents a general contribution to advance research on multi-attribute decision-making, as it allows modeling attribute-specific attentional discounting, which is likely to occur if attributes are described in markedly different formats.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Attribute-specific attentional discounting is likely to occur if attributes are described in markedly different formats.
source: This modeling extension represents a general contribution to advance research on multi-attribute decision-making, as it allows modeling attribute-specific attentional discounting, which is likely to occur if attributes are described in markedly different formats.
evidence: This is a speculation about when the model would be applicable.

claim: The study was preregistered on Open Science Framework.
source: The study was preregistered on Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/tmdw3/).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: An a-priori power analysis was conducted to determine the required sample size of the experiment using G*Power.
source: An a-priori power analysis was conducted to determine the required sample size of the experiment using G*Power (Faul et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: The required sample size for a one-tailed paired t-test was 70 participants.
source: Given inflated effect sizes due to publication bias (Simonsohn, 2015), we set our smallest effect size of interest (Lakens et al., 2018) to Cohen's d=0.3, with an alpha level of 0.05, and a power of 0.8, resulting in a required sample size for a one-tailed paired t-test of 70 participants.
evidence: This is based on power analysis calculations.

claim: The current experiment is sufficiently powered.
source: In line with Skrynka and Vincent, 2019, we expected a larger effect of hunger on food choices (i.e. d=0.5) and thus consider the current experiment being sufficiently powered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the power analysis and expected effect sizes.

claim: The Local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Human Movement Sciences at the University of Hamburg approved the study.
source: The Local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Human Movement Sciences at the University of Hamburg approved the study.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: In the sated condition, participants received a protein shake matched to their daily caloric needs.
source: In the sated condition, participants received an individually determined amount of whey protein shake from MyProtein (https://www.myprotein.com/) (flavor: vanilla, or strawberry) amounting to 25% of participants' daily caloric needs in line with Schofield equations (Schofield, 1985).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The experiment was implemented in OpenSesame version 3.3.
source: The experiment was implemented in OpenSesame version 3.3 (Mathôt et al., 2012), and PyGaze (Dalmaijer et al., 2014) was used for the implementation of different eye-tracking functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental software.

claim: Stimuli of the food tasks were taken from the Full4Health Image Collection.
source: Stimuli of the food tasks were taken from the Full4Health Image Collection and included 66 standardized images of food presented on a plate (Charbonnier et al., 2016, available at https://osf.io/cx7tp/).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental stimuli.

claim: Participants were asked to select the food image they preferred, knowing that they would be incentivized in line with their choices.
source: In the binary food choice task, participants were asked to select the food image they preferred, knowing that they would be incentivized in line with their choices (see Incentivization).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: During the choice tasks, participants' fixation patterns were recorded using a SR Research EyeLink 1000 Plus eye-tracker.
source: During the choice tasks, participants' fixation patterns were recorded using a SR Research EyeLink 1000 Plus eye-tracker for high-quality recording of eye movements and pupillometry with up to 2 kHz sampling rate.
evidence: This is a statement about the eye-tracking equipment.

claim: Preprocessing of eye-tracking data was performed in Matlab.
source: Preprocessing of eye-tracking data was performed in Matlab (2021b, https://www.mathworks.com/) using the edfmex converter (SR Research Ltd.).
evidence: This is a statement about the data preprocessing.

claim: RTs were preprocessed by excluding trials that were >4 SD above the individual mean RT per condition or <250 ms.
source: In line with our preregistration, RTs were preprocessed before further analyses by excluding trials that were >4 SD above the individual mean RT per condition or <250 ms.
evidence: This is a statement about the data preprocessing.

claim: The analysis of the hunger state manipulation had a sample size of 64 due to missing data.
source: Due to missing data in the VAS and PANAS at timepoint 1 (i.e. upon arrival at the lab) in six participants, the analysis of the hunger state manipulation had a sample size of 64.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample size for a specific analysis.

claim: The main analyses comprised two types of generalized linear mixed models using the lme4 package in R.
source: The main analyses comprised two types of generalized linear mixed models (GLMM) using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) in R (version: 4.3.1).
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical analysis.

claim: The eye-tracking analyses were implemented on conflicting trials.
source: The eye-tracking analyses were implemented on conflicting trials (i.e. one option was tastier compared to the other option).
evidence: This is a statement about the analysis approach.

claim: The computational models were fit to choices and RT of all pre-processed trials.
source: The computational models were fit to choices and RT of all (pre-processed) trials.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: Hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation was performed with JAGS, called within R using the R2jags package.
source: Hierarchical Bayesian parameter estimation (Farrell and Lewandowsky, 2018) was performed with JAGS, called within R using the R2jags package (Su and Yajima, 2021), and accelerated by parallel computing.
evidence: This is a statement about the parameter estimation method.

claim: Piecewise constant averaging was used to speed up model fit.
source: We used piecewise constant averaging (Lombardi and Hare, 2021) to speed up model fit, in particular, of the (ma)aDDMs.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach.

claim: Model fit was quantified with the Deviance Information Criterion.
source: Model fit was quantified with the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) (Spiegelhalter et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a statement about the model comparison method.

claim: Parameter recoveries were implemented for the best models.
source: We implemented parameter recoveries of our best models (Appendix 10—figures 1–4).
evidence: This is a statement about the model validation approach.
